Why did my multi-line function definition break?
A line with just `/` on it swallowed the rest of my file.

A `/` alone on a line opens a BLOCK comment that runs until a lone `\` closes it -- that is a K convention, not a typo in your file. A line comment needs text after the slash:

    / this is a comment

and a trailing comment needs a space before the slash, because `x/y` with no space is the over adverb.
Why is my one-argument lambda suddenly asking for two?

Because it mentions `y`. Amber infers a lambda's arity from the implicit names it uses: a body that references `y` anywhere is dyadic, even if the reference is dead code. `f:{y}` then `f 1` gives you the projection `{y}[1;]` rather than a value.

Use `x` only for a monadic function, or name the parameters explicitly: `{[a]a+1}`.
I named a variable `cols` and everything broke.

`cols` is a standard-library verb -- `cols:{$[iskeyed x;(!!x),!.x;!x]}` in amber.k -- and assigning to the name shadows it for the rest of the session, including inside qsql.k, which calls `cols` on every query.

The same applies to `sum`, `count`, `max`, `min`, `first`, `last`, `in`, `key`, `value`, `type`, `string`, `like`, `ss` and `bar`. Check with `cols` on its own: if it prints a lambda, the name is still the library's.
Does Amber support octal escapes in strings?

No. `"\101"` is the three characters `1`, `0`, `1` -- the backslash is dropped and nothing is decoded. Only `\n`, `\t`, `\r`, `\\` and `\"` are escapes.

To build a character from its code point, cast: `` `c$65 `` is "A". To go the other way, `0+"a"` is 97.
What type is a keyed table?

`` `m `` -- a DICTIONARY. A keyed table is a dictionary whose keys are a table and whose values are a table, which is why `!kt` gives the key table and `. kt` the value table, and why `iskeyed` has to test `` `M=@!x `` rather than just look at the outer type.

An unkeyed table is `` `M ``.
Why does `istable . x` behave oddly?

`istable . x` is not `istable(. x)` -- `.` between two values is DYADIC APPLY, so the parser reads it as applying `istable` to the argument list `x`. On a table that runs away and raises 'limit.

Parenthesise when you mean the monadic `.`: `istable(. x)`. Or just write `istable x`.
Is `0N!x` a print statement?
No. `0N!x` is modulo by a null and quietly returns zeros. Amber's print verbs are `show x` for a formatted value and `` `0:"text" `` for a raw string.
What is the difference between `01b` in kdb+ and in Amber?

In Amber `01b` is the integer vector `0 1`, not a distinct boolean type. Comparisons return integers too, which is why you can index a list with a predicate: `` `lo`hi@px>190 `` works because `px>190` is a vector of 0s and 1s.
Why do I get a projection instead of a result?

Because you supplied fewer arguments than the lambda's arity. Amber curries: `{x+y}[1]` is a one-argument function waiting for `y`, printed as `{x+y}[1;]`. Supply both -- `{x+y}[1;2]` -- or elide the one you want to leave open on purpose: `like[;"A*"]` is a deliberate projection, and it is what lets `each` drive it.
Does the `where` clause run row by row?

No, and that is the point. qsql.k compiles the predicate into a one-argument function with every column name rewritten to `x`col`, then calls it ONCE with the whole table. `px>200` is a vector comparison over the entire column, and the boolean vector it returns is what selects the rows.

So a `where` clause can use any vector expression, but it cannot use anything that only makes sense for a single row -- there is no current row.
Does `update` modify my table?

No. `upd` builds and returns a NEW table; the original name is untouched. To keep the result you have to bind it:

    trades:update notional:px*sz from trades

The same is true of `delete`, `xasc`, `sortcol` and every other table helper -- they are functions returning values, not statements with side effects.
Why does my time column print as a number in one table and a clock in another?

Because the rendering is keyed on the column NAME, not on a datatype. amber.k renders an integer column as HH:MM:SS.mmm when its name is in `TCOLS` (`` `time`ts`t ``) and as YYYY.MM.DD when it is in `DCOLS` (`` `date ``). Rename the column and the formatting goes away; the value never changes either way.

To force the clock rendering on any column, `tsym[t;c]` converts it to strings. To turn the automatic behaviour off, set `TCOLS:0#`.
How many rows does a grid print before truncating?
Twenty, then a `..` line and the row count. `CROWS` holds the limit, and the cap is applied BEFORE formatting, so printing a huge table is cheap. Set `CROWS:100` to see more.
Why is `sum` of an empty vector not always 0?

It is 0, but of the right TYPE: `sum 0#0` is the integer 0 and `sum 0#0.0` is the float 0.0. amber.k special-cases the empty case precisely so an empty float column does not silently become an integer and change the type of everything downstream.
What is the empty general list, and why does it matter?

`()` is the untyped empty list, and it is what a C kernel returns when it declines an input -- that is how std.k's `msum` knows to fall back to its K definition, by testing `` `A~@r ``. It is not the same as `0#0` (an empty int vector) or `0#0.0` (an empty float vector), and the difference survives into aggregates.
Are comparisons chainable, like `1<x<10`?

No -- and the result is silently wrong rather than an error. Right to left, `1<x<10` is `1<(x<10)`, which compares 1 against a vector of 0s and 1s and is therefore all-false.

Write the two comparisons out and join them: `(1<v)&v<10`.

Right-to-left evaluation. `180&px<200` runs first -- an element-wise MIN of 180 against a 0/1 vector, which is just that vector -- and only then is it compared with `px`. Parenthesise the first comparison.
